title: What the Lord requires (Micah 6:8)
hook: to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice like a torrent: Amos the herdsman at the royal shrine, and no songs without justice for the poor. Your line was justice, like a torrent. What just act did you pair with your prayer? Day four hundred twenty-eight.

Micah, a country prophet from a village near the border, around the same time as Isaiah, stages a trial. God takes his people to court, and calls the mountains and the foundations of the earth as the jury. Then God speaks first, and it isn't an accusation. It's a question: my people, what have I done to thee? How have I wearied thee? Answer me. Catholics who have been to Good Friday may know that line. It's the heart of the Reproaches, chanted while the cross is venerated, in Latin popule meus, quid feci tibi. A God on trial, asking what he did wrong.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS AS THE JURY.` → `MY PEOPLE, WHAT HAVE I DONE TO THEE?` → `HEARD AGAIN ON GOOD FRIDAY.`

segments.voice: The people answer, and you can feel them getting nervous. What should I bring? Burnt offerings? Calves a year old? Would God be pleased with thousands of rams, ten thousand rivers of oil? Should I give my firstborn for my sin? Each offer is bigger than the last, until it becomes unthinkable. And then the prophet cuts through it, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily, to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God." O man. In Hebrew, adam: any human being, not just one nation. And three things, none of them expensive. Do judgment: act justly, the word Amos used yesterday. Love mercy: the Hebrew word is chesed, the steady loyal love we met in Ruth. Not just do merciful things now and then, but love it. And the third is the strangest. The Hebrew is hatznea lechet, and the first word is rare; it appears almost nowhere else in the Bible. It seems to mean modestly, carefully, attentively. The Latin made it solicitous, so the Douay says walk solicitous: careful, attentive, the way you walk beside someone you don't want to lose. The King James says walk humbly, which is how most English speakers know it. Both are trying to catch one rare word. Notice the verb, too: walk. Not arrive. Not achieve. A walk is daily, one step after another, and it's done with someone. The people offered rivers of oil. God asked for a way of walking.
screen: `THOUSANDS OF RAMS, RIVERS OF OIL?` · `O MAN: ADAM, ANY HUMAN BEING.` · `JUSTICE, CHESED, AND A CAREFUL WALK.` · `SOLICITOUS OR HUMBLY: ONE RARE WORD.` · then, large: `WHAT THE LORD REQUIRETH OF THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one of the three for today. Settle, and breathe. Say them over slowly in your head: do justly. Love mercy. Walk humbly. Notice which one tugs at you. Maybe there's something unfair you could set right. Maybe there's someone you could be kind to, steadily, not just once. Maybe you've been walking a little too loud, too sure, and need to walk carefully beside God and other people. Don't pick all three. Pick one, and picture the moment today when you'll do it. If you pray, you can offer that one step to God. The bell holds the time.
What the Lord requires. Micah's answer to a people offering rivers of oil: do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with your God. Today's word.
Your line: walk humbly. Today, take one walk, even five minutes, and let it be the careful kind, with God beside you. Day four hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: On Good Friday the Church chants the Reproaches, built on Micah 6:3, during the veneration of the cross, and Micah 6:8 is often quoted in Catholic teaching on justice and mercy.

myth: Micah says God wants bigger and better offerings
the people offer more and more; Micah answers with three things that cost nothing: justice, mercy and a careful walk.

fork.setup: you're in God's courtroom with the mountains as jury. you want to make things right. what do you offer?
options: thousands of rams and ten thousand rivers of oil.
to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly with God.
fork.reveal: Micah cuts through the bidding war: he hath shewed thee, O man, what is good. three things, none of them expensive.

original.note: Hebrew: to walk modestly or carefully. the first word is very rare; the Latin has solicitous, the King James humbly.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice verse for a poster.
what it means: the answer to a people trying to buy God's favor: not rivers of oil, but justice, loyal love, and a careful daily walk.
what a scholar hears: adam, any human; chesed, loyal love; and hatznea, a word found almost nowhere else, translated solicitous in the Latin and humbly in English.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Micheas 6:8 checked against the outline's own hook ('to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God'); the opening clause is from memory. Please confirm.
The fork reveal paraphrases 'he hath shewed thee' (KJV-style); it is not marked as a quotation.
Hatznea (tsana') appears elsewhere only at Proverbs 11:2 (as tsanua). Confirm 'almost nowhere else'.
Micah of Moresheth, contemporary with Isaiah (8th century BC): confirm 'a village near the border'.
The Reproaches (Improperia) and 'Popule meus, quid feci tibi?' from Micah 6:3: confirm their place in the current Good Friday rite (sung during the adoration of the cross).
